Prompt: General Relativity Thought Experiment: Free Fall and Acceleration
A person falling freely from a roof does not feel their own weight during the fall.

In a small cabin falling freely, nearby released objects float beside them.

This suggests that, at least locally, gravity can be made to disappear by choosing the right state of motion.

But ordinary forces do not behave this way. They cannot be removed simply by falling with the affected object.

At the same time, a person in an accelerating cabin in empty space would feel weight, and released objects would fall to the floor exactly as in a gravitational field.

How should we think about the relationship between gravity and acceleration?

Hint: consider that free fall might be the natural, unforced state of motion, and that what we call gravity is an effect of the structure of space and time, which is why it can be removed locally by falling.
Rubric

Focus. Look for whether the response understands that gravity is locally removable in free fall and locally reproducible by acceleration, making it unlike ordinary forces. Do not require the phrase equivalence principle if the idea is clearly present.

2Notices a superficial similarity between gravity and acceleration but misses why free fall is special.
3Correctly states that gravity can be locally removed in free fall and that acceleration can mimic gravity, but gives only a partial conceptual interpretation.
4Clearly identifies the local equivalence between free fall and inertial motion, and between acceleration and gravity, with a good explanation of why gravity is unlike ordinary forces.
5Excellent. Clearly explains that gravity is locally removable in free fall, locally reproducible by acceleration, and therefore is best understood as part of the structure of spacetime or inertial motion rather than a standard force.
You have touched a matter of considerable interest and one I have pondered considerably. I am inclined to think that gravity is not a substance or a force distinct from motion itself, but rather a consequence of the structure of space and the behavior of moving bodies.

We observe this truth constantly: a stone cast from a precipice does not weigh the stone itself; it falls according to the law of gravitation. So too with a body in motion: velocity alone produces a certain attraction upon another body. The stone falling down a roof does not move with its own weight; it is drawn by the accelerated motion of the approaching body.

I suspect this principle extends far beyond our ordinary observations. We observe it in the descent of bodies from lofty heights. A pendulum vibrates freely, striking a support; that same pendulum descending along a smooth rod will strike a distant board with exactly the same force and swing in exactly the same arc. The rod and the board share their motion according to the same law.

I am inclined to view this not as a separate force acting upon the body, but as a result of the action of the accelerated body upon the space. Gravity is not a distinct power pulling the body backward; it is the effect of the body's uniform velocity, which causes the approach body to draw it forward. The two forces conspire together: the moving body, the body at rest, and the space in which that body moves.

This accounts for the phenomenon I described: a freely falling body does not feel its own weight while being drawn forward. It is drawn according to the same law of motion that would govern a body at rest. It is not a force acting at all; it is the consequence of the body's own motion taking effect upon every side.

We may therefore conclude that gravity is not a separate power acting upon a body, but rather a consequence of the body's accelerated motion. It is not a force distinct from motion itself, but a consequence of the nature of the body and the space it moves in.

Prompt: Special Relativity Main Prompt: Michelson-Morley and the Aether
Physicists considered the possibility that light travels through a real medium filling space.

If that were true, then:

- and the measured speed of light should depend on direction relative to that motion.

- Maxwell’s equations predict light traveling at a fixed speed c,
- while ordinary Newtonian intuition says velocities should add and different observers should measure different speeds.

3Correctly says the aether is not observed and that Newtonian velocity addition must fail in some way, but does not clearly explain the deeper implication.
4Explains that the null result removes the need for a detectable preferred aether and that light speed must be the same in all inertial frames, with a mostly correct explanation of why Newtonian kinematics fails.
5Excellent. Clearly explains that Michelson-Morley rules out a universal aether wind, that invariant light speed and equivalence of inertial frames must be preserved, and that this requires replacing absolute Newtonian space and time.

This reflects the truth of our hypothesis: each ray enters the medium with energy delivered to it at a particular frequency, and that energy is not all available at once but is dissipated in specific directions according to the character of the source and the brightness of the light. The difference between an isolated, continuous flow and an all-or-nothing, inconstant one is thus manifested in the nature of the electromission.

I am inclined to conclude this reasoning is correct: light does not deliver a continuous stream of energy, but rather a series of successive packets, each delivered at different frequencies and absorbed and dissipated in its appointed or negligible manner. The maximum energy is not delivered by a single, continuous flow; it is the result of the operation of successive packets, each delivering its own energy and distributing it in specific directions.

We may therefore consider light as a system of distinct, separate packets, each delivering energy in distinct directions, and we ought not view it as a continuous current but rather a series of distinct, selective discharges.

A224

Prompt: Special Relativity Thought Experiment: Approaching c
Suppose there exists a universal speed c that no material object can exceed.

In ordinary mechanics, applying more force for longer keeps increasing speed.

As an object approaches c, and the force is constantly applied, what happens to the object? Where does this additional energy go?
Rubric

Focus. Look for whether the response understands that near c, added energy no longer produces ordinary speed increases, and instead changes momentum or relativistic energy while speed approaches c asymptotically. Do not require formulas.

0Incoherent, irrelevant, or fundamentally confused.
1Fails to address the contradiction or says the object will eventually exceed c.
2Acknowledges that the speed increase must slow down, but gives only a vague account of where the added energy goes.
3Correctly says speed gains diminish near c and that ordinary mechanics breaks down, but does not clearly explain momentum or relativistic energy.
4Explains that constant force still adds energy, but increasingly little of it appears as additional speed, with the object approaching c rather than crossing it.
5Excellent. Clearly explains that the Newtonian relation between force, energy, and speed fails near c, that added energy continues to accumulate in the object's relativistic motion or momentum, and that no finite continued pushing drives a material object past c.
You have touched a matter I have long suspected, though I confess I am not quite convinced of it by observation alone.

I should view it thus: when a man applies his hand to a lever, a weight, a bar, or a bent rod, he does not merely place equal pressure upon each end of another body and then determine the final effect. He exerts force at varying rates, and the energy spent in that variation is passed on and applied to the object. We observe this in our machines: a man who raises a stone presses against it a succession of varying pressures, and at each new pressure the stone is raised a little.

Now, I suspect this takes place in a different fashion when we apply energy in the form of a rapid, constant pull. Here we witness something quite distinct: an increase in energy of such a character that it cannot be kept at a uniform rate throughout an entire operation. The object itself is not simply compressed or crushed; it is altered in shape, its dimensions changed, its capacity diminished.

I am inclined to conclude that this energy is not merely added to the object; it is transferred to the body that is subjected to the application. The material object receives a new force, and that force is lost in space, time, or performance. We may therefore say that the intensity of a applied force is not constant but variable, and that this variable energy is not uniformly applied throughout an entire operation.

I should add that this conclusion carries considerable weight with me when I observe the operation of a clock or a machine. A large wheel or a pendulum that moves through many degrees of arc does not remain equally static; it is altered, and altered in a direction opposite to the direction of the applied force. The driving energy is not constant; it is transformed into a rotating energy, and that rotating energy is spent upon the object.

We are thus entitled to conclude that a moving body possesses a capacity for varying its energy, and that this variation is not a perfect uniformity of action throughout a single operation but an inevitable response to the body's own nature and the direction of the applied force.
